title: Is the nature of leadership changing?
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart works through Michael Fullan's claim that the nature of school leadership is changing, organised around Fullan's four components: experts in context, joint determination, a culture of accountability and becoming a system player. Using the example of a deputy head who moves schools and loses much of their effectiveness overnight, he argues that leadership expertise depends heavily on contextual knowledge, especially of colleagues' underlying beliefs and assumptions, which is gained mainly by talking. Drawing on Neil Gilbride, he suggests knowledge can be a disrupting experience that stimulates leaders' ego development. He then follows Fullan and Louise Stoll in arguing that complex problems require joint problem-solving through dialogue, and that school improvement is fundamentally individual and organisational learning. On accountability he emphasises internal accountability built by modelling common values in the work of instruction rather than by external pressure. Finally he argues that leaders must look outside their school to avoid echo chambers, likening it to sharpening the axe. He concludes that knowledge is integral to leadership expertise but insufficient without collective understanding and purpose.
points: Expertise in school leadership is heavily contextual: a skilled deputy head who changes schools must rapidly rebuild knowledge of community, colleagues and their beliefs to be effective again.
Hart argues knowledge does not simply unlock solutions but helps leaders appreciate the problems more fully, and can itself be a disrupting experience that drives ego development.
Following Fullan and Stoll, the more complex the problem the more people should be part of the solution, with dialogue as the engine of collective learning.
Internal accountability, built by modelling shared values in instructional work, matters more than external accountability.
Leaders should invest time outside their own school to avoid echo chambers and plateaued practice, the 'sharpening the axe' argument for system leadership.
quotes: The deputy headteacher still knows all about safeguarding procedures, curriculum design, what makes great teaching etc but their contextual knowledge of the new school needs to be built, and quickly, if they are going to be as effective in their new school as they were in their previous school.

Knowledge isn’t necessarily the key that, once leaders acquire, enables them to solve complex problems of school improvement. Rather, knowledge helps us to more fully appreciate the problems that we are trying to solve.

An area of contextual knowledge not made explicit by Leithwood et al above is the underlying beliefs and assumptions held by colleagues and they are important because they are what sustains people’s actions.

Fullan warns of the increasing complexity of change dynamics and advises that leaders must be close to the action in order to adapt and resolve issues. Being close to the action is certainly achievable through the dialogue and learning conversations that Stoll advocates.

Individual schools can easily become echo chambers where our practice plateaus while there is likely to be countless other leaders in similar contexts going about the work differently that we can learn from.
It might take time away from chopping wood to sharpen an axe but is worth it in the long run. So to the practice becoming a system player.

Our understanding of the complexity of school leadership certainly is, along with the integral role of knowledge in school leadership expertise. But knowledge alone is insufficient. Collective understanding and purpose surely is at the heart of continuous school improvement.
